decision.location: Results, lines 1918-1926 (see also Methods lines 1453-1505; Discussion lines 2193-2201; References lines 2483-2487)
decision.quote:
We also tested the hypothesis that children with DLD were less likely in the QHP task to 

reach across the midline with the right hand to a spatial position on the left side of the body, 

indicating weaker hand preference, as previously reported (Bishop, 2005; E. L. Hill & Bishop, 

1998). A multilevel model was run with twin pair membership as a random effect, group as a 

between factor and spatial position as a within factor.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work (never previously adjudicated). The source text explicitly re-tests the finding of Bishop (2005) (doi:10.1002/dev.20062) that developmental language disorder (SLI/DLD) is associated with a reduced tendency to reach across the midline with the right hand on the Quantification of Hand Preference (QHP) task. This empirical replication test is specified in Methods (lines 1453-1505), executed via multilevel modeling in Results (lines 1918-1960), and evaluated in the Discussion (lines 2193-2201). It is an independent original study (6-year-old twins in Developmental Psychobiology) distinct from shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008, adult fTCD cerebral dominance) and from sibling target 1 (Hill & Bishop, 1998, clinical SLI/DCD sample in Laterality).

corrected_value.authors: Illingworth, S., & Bishop, D. V. M.
corrected_value.title: Atypical cerebral lateralisation in adults with compensated developmental dyslexia demonstrated using functional transcranial Doppler ultrasound

decision.location: Conclusions, lines 2385-2395 (see also Methods lines 1281-1295; Discussion lines 2183-2189; References lines 2869-2875)
decision.quote:
In a large sample of twins oversampled for language problems, the present study failed to 

find evidence for atypical laterality, either in terms of handedness or cerebral lateralisation for 

language, in those with DLD. Theories have proposed that disruption to the typical left 

hemisphere dominance for language may be a neurobiological correlate of language problems 

(e.g. Annett, 2002; Bishop, 2013; T. J. Crow et al., 1998), and empirical studies of very small 

samples have supported that view (Illingworth & Bishop, 2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008).
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. In Methods (lines 1281-1295), the authors explicitly include children impaired on literacy measures in the DLD group on the basis of Illingworth & Bishop's (2009) fTCD finding of reduced left-hemisphere language lateralisation in dyslexia, and in both the Discussion (lines 2183-2189) and Conclusions (lines 2385-2415) they explicitly state that their fTCD comparison failed to replicate the reduced left-hemisphere language dominance reported by Illingworth & Bishop (2009) (doi:10.1016/j.bandl.2009.05.002) and Whitehouse & Bishop (2008). Because shipped row 2411 captures only Whitehouse & Bishop (2008) (blind target 3), Illingworth & Bishop (2009) is a genuinely distinct missing replication target.

decision.location: Discussion, lines 2183-2189 (see also Introduction lines 359-375; Conclusions lines 2385-2398)
decision.quote:
Based on our large 

sample size, we suggest that previous reports of reduced left hemispheric dominance for 

language among those with language problems in smaller studies (e.g. Illingworth & Bishop, 

2009; Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008) are likely to have been false positives.
decision.reason: Resolving the Luna hold on target 4: Bishop, Holt, Whitehouse, & Groen (2014) (doi:10.7717/peerj.507) is cited only once in the Introduction literature review (lines 361-375, noting that n=11 four-year-olds with language problems did not show a statistically significant group-level left bias) alongside background fMRI studies (e.g., Guibert et al., 2011; Bernal & Altman, 2003). Unlike Illingworth & Bishop (2009) (target 2) and Whitehouse & Bishop (2008) (shipped row 2411 / target 3), Bishop et al. (2014) is never cited in the Methods, Results, Discussion, or Conclusions as a finding re-tested by the present study. Instead, the Discussion (lines 2183-2189) and Conclusions (lines 2385-2415) explicitly identify Illingworth & Bishop (2009) and Whitehouse & Bishop (2008) as the prior fTCD reports of reduced left-hemisphere dominance evaluated and not replicated here.

decision.location: Methods, lines 1527-1535 (see also Results lines 2081-2107; References lines 2777-2785)
decision.quote:
A subsidiary aim was to see whether we could replicate associations between language 

laterality and language tests found by Groen et al. (2012). Analysis was conducted in two 

replication samples, as described above, so that data from only one twin of each twin pair 

contributed to each analysis. Spearman's method was used, since the laterality index is not 

normally distributed, and all 13 language measures as well as performance IQ were included.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent for this work. Both the Methods (lines 1527-1545) and Results (lines 2081-2107) explicitly state a subsidiary replication aim to re-test the continuous associations between fTCD language laterality and language test performance reported by Groen et al. (2012) (doi:10.1002/brb3.56) by computing Spearman's correlations across two twin replication subsamples. This is a distinct original study and empirical replication test not represented by shipped row 2411 (Whitehouse & Bishop, 2008) or any other sibling target.

decision.location: Introduction, line 90 (see also lines 91, 95; Discussion lines 463-466, 472, 475; References lines 491, 497)
decision.quote: Tracked for four years, dysregulated fear was associated with greater social withdrawal (Buss, 2011) throughout the preschool years and kindergarten, as well as social anxiety disorder symptoms (Buss et al., 2013) at 6 years, compared to a more normative fear profile.
decision.reason: In the prior adjudication for c931e17eb50f6ca0, shipped input_row_index 418 was corrected to Buss (2011) (doi:10.1037/a0023227, blind target 0), while target 1 (Buss et al., 2013) was marked blind_right with an invalid schema payload. Independent source review shows that Buss (2011) and Buss et al. (2013) are same-study follow-up waves of the exact same original cohort of N = 111 toddlers ('Tracked for four years, dysregulated fear was associated with greater social withdrawal (Buss, 2011) throughout the preschool years and kindergarten, as well as social anxiety disorder symptoms (Buss et al., 2013) at 6 years'; referred to in the singular throughout as 'a low risk, community sample', 'In the original sample', 'In the previous cohort', and contrasted with the present study's 'second cohort of children', lines 90-95, 464-465, 475). Furthermore, the present study only followed its second cohort from 24 to 48 months (preschool: ages 2, 3, and 4 years) and tested only (1) identification of the 24-month dysregulated fear pattern (Buss, 2011) and (2) its longitudinal association with parent-reported social inhibition across preschool at 24, 36, and 48 months (already reported for the original cohort in Buss, 2011), without following children to kindergarten (age 6) or assessing social anxiety disorder symptoms ('to date we have only followed these children into early childhood', line 472). Because target 1 is a same-cohort follow-up citation whose retested preschool social-inhibition finding is already represented by Buss (2011) (target 0 / corrected row 418), retaining a second row would duplicate the same original study and retested finding.
